name: Salt water rinse

lead: A salt water rinse is a homemade mouthwash of warm water with dissolved salt. People use it to soothe sore gums and keep the mouth clean, for healthier gums and a fresher mouth at almost no cost.

Wikipedia describes saline as a mechanical cleanser with antiseptic action, because the solution is hypertonic to bacteria. A school-based randomised trial compared salt water with chlorhexidine for effects on dental plaque and oral microbes.

paras: People mix salt into warm water at home and swish it gently, often after meals or brushing, or when gums feel sore. It is commonly used alongside regular brushing and flossing.
Low risk. After dental extractions, guidance advises holding the rinse gently at first rather than swishing vigorously.

angle.text: Warm salt water rinses are a low-cost home habit for soothing sore gums and keeping the mouth clean, supporting healthier gums and a fresher mouth. Saline is described as a mechanical cleanser with antiseptic action, and one school trial compared it with chlorhexidine.

lead: A salt water rinse is warm water with dissolved salt, swished around the mouth as a low-cost mouthwash. People use it to keep gums comfortable and the mouth clean, supporting fresher breath and a healthier-looking smile alongside brushing.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes saline as a mechanical cleanser with antiseptic action, because it is hypertonic to bacteria, and notes that warm solutions increase blood flow to the area, which may aid healing.[1] A homemade version can combine salt with baking soda.[1]

A randomized trial in 30 participants found that salt water rinsing for five days reduced plaque and salivary microbial counts, matching chlorhexidine for plaque reduction and for one bacterium, while chlorhexidine performed better against three others. The authors concluded it can serve as an adjunct to routine mechanical plaque control.[2]
infobox: Soothing gums, cleaning the mouth, after-extraction mouth baths

paras: The rinse is made by dissolving salt in warm water. Saline cleans mechanically and acts as an antiseptic; it is hypertonic to bacteria and is described as causing them to burst.[1] It is also noted as an option for people sensitive to the ingredients in commercial mouthwash.[1]

Salt water gargles appear in early accounts: Hippocrates recommended a mixture of salt, alum and vinegar, ancient Chinese records describe gargling salt water, tea and wine for antiseptic effect, and peoples of the Americas used salt water for sore throats, though dating is imprecise.[1]

A 2017 school-based randomized controlled trial in the Journal of the Indian Society of Pedodontics and Preventive Dentistry first measured the minimum inhibitory concentration of salt water against four oral bacteria, then randomized 30 participants to salt water or chlorhexidine rinsing for five days after prophylaxis. Both groups had significant reductions in plaque and salivary microbial counts; salt water performed as well as chlorhexidine for plaque and for A. actinomycetemcomitans, while chlorhexidine was significantly better against S. mutans, L. acidophilus and P. gingivalis.[2]
Wikipedia notes current guidelines that saline works about as well as other rinses for pain and healing time in oral mucositis from cancer therapy.[1]

After tooth extraction, dental guidance cited by Wikipedia is to begin warm salt water mouth baths about 24 hours later, holding the liquid passively at first so the blood clot is not dislodged.[1] Wikipedia also notes that alcohol-containing commercial mouthwashes can dry the mouth, which can encourage odor-producing bacteria; salt water contains no alcohol.[1]

lore.intro: Salt water is discussed in lifestyle and training forums as an inexpensive home remedy.[3]
